endorsements.quote: When AI solutions are intended for direct patient use, it is essential to employ human factors design methods to comprehend both the capabilities and constraints of the end users.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Understanding users and their needs and limitations should occur early in the 1650 development process for the AI-enabled device and may be repeated as the design process 1651 continues.

evidence.title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.effect: revealed older adults required explicit guidance for initiating interactions
evidence.quote: Participatory cocreation workshops revealed that older adults required explicit guidance for initiating interactions, leading to a short video tutorial on dialogue initiation (Fig. 1b ).

commentary.bottom_line: One randomized trial of 2,113 participants in China found that early user-needs work identified a need among older adults for explicit guidance to start interactions with the tool, which supports the practice. Four sources endorse the practice, including FDA draft guidance, but the evidence rests on a single study conducted outside the United States.

perspectives.view: A single randomized trial (n=2113) in a real deployment supports the practice. Certainty is low for three reasons. One study cannot show consistency. The report describes a needs-identification finding rather than a measured effect on outcomes. The Chinese setting limits directness for US health systems. No study documenting the hazard was supplied.

The trial found that older adults required explicit guidance to begin interactions, and design reviews without user input may miss needs of this kind. The supplied evidence does not show whether acting on the finding reduced errors, automation bias, or harm. The safety benefit therefore remains an inference.

The needs assessment took place within a real deployment, which suggests it can run alongside routine use. The report does not describe how often needs were reassessed during design, how much staff time the work required, or how the findings changed the tool. Fidelity and burden therefore cannot be judged.

The trial enrolled older, rural, low health literacy, non-English-speaking, and minority participants, who are the groups the recommendation aims to protect. It was conducted in China and included no US Medicaid or safety-net setting. How well the findings transfer to those US populations is uncertain.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that understanding users' needs and limitations should occur early in development and may be repeated. CHAI treats the practice as a must for patient-facing tools. These sources are endorsements, and the single supplied trial gives limited empirical support for their specific requirements.

Older adults in the trial needed explicit prompts to start using the tool. This suggests that some patients may be unable to begin an interaction without that help. The trial does not report whether patients could reach a human when the tool did not meet their needs.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared tools built with and without human factors methods on usability, error rates, automation bias, or patient harm. No study tested whether reassessing users' needs repeatedly across the design cycle adds value beyond a single early assessment. Trials in US Medicaid, safety-net, and limited English proficiency populations have not been reported.
commentary.underserved_note: The one trial included participants with low health literacy, non-English language, rural residence, minority status, and older age. It was conducted in China and did not involve US Medicaid or safety-net settings. The finding may inform design for similar groups, but US health systems serving these populations lack direct evidence.
